drafts.title: Improve ride comfort over broken pavement
drafts.description: Customers experience a smooth, non‑jarring ride on broken or uneven pavement so that short road defects do not feel harsh or cause discomfort for driver and passengers.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: On a 500 m section of standardized broken-pavement test (representative of typical US secondary roads) driven at 30 mph, in a panel of 30 occupants the median discomfort rating on a 5‑point scale is ≤2 and ≤20% of occupants rate the ride as 'uncomfortable' or worse.
assumptions: Test uses a repeatable published rough-road profile representative of customer reports.
Production suspension and damping hardware remain within current packaging and cost targets.
uncertainties: Trade-offs between more comfort on broken pavement and dynamic body control (roll, pitch) in sporty driving.
Variability in road surfaces across markets may require calibration variants.

drafts.title: Reduce distracting wind noise at highway speeds
drafts.description: At highway speeds customers perceive wind noise as quiet and non‑distracting so long drives above 70 mph do not create fatigue or require raising audio volume.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Interior A‑weighted sound level at the driver's ear is ≤68 dB(A) at 75 mph on a certified highway wind‑noise route (windows closed, sunroof closed).
assumptions: Measurement carried out with standard production glass and mirror configurations.
Target measured in neutral crosswind conditions defined by the test protocol.
uncertainties: Extreme crosswinds or aftermarket roof accessories may increase measured levels.
Some aerodynamic changes could affect fuel/energy consumption slightly.

drafts.title: Make lane keeping assist smooth and non‑startling in curves
drafts.description: When lane keeping assist intervenes in curves customers feel the steering corrections are smooth and predictable, not abrupt or surprising.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In a validation of 100 representative highway curve events (40–70 mph) with 30 drivers, ≤10% of lane-keeping interventions are rated 'abrupt' by the driver on a 3‑point abruptness scale.
assumptions: Validation uses representative highway curves and typical tire/wheel options.
Driver interface informs driver of system status in accordance with current HMI norms.
uncertainties: Perception of 'abrupt' varies between drivers and across vehicle configurations.
Tuning for smoother interventions may modestly reduce lane-centering precision in some edge cases.

drafts.title: Show charging state at a glance via the charge port light
drafts.description: Customers can identify the vehicle's charging state quickly from outside the car using the charge-port light so they don’t need to open an app or crowd the port.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: From 3 meters and up to a 45° horizontal viewing angle in daylight, users can correctly identify one of three states (charging, fully charged, fault) within 3 seconds with ≥95% accuracy in a user test of 30 participants.
assumptions: Charge-port light uses visible LED signalling and consistent color/flash semantics.
Test includes daytime and twilight lighting conditions typical for customers.
uncertainties: Extreme glare or damaged lights may reduce recognition accuracy.
Color-blind users may rely on flashing patterns rather than color; patterns must be distinct.

drafts.title: Help customers find compatible fast chargers reliably on trips
drafts.description: When customers plan long trips the car shows chargers that are compatible with the vehicle and highlights estimated availability so locating a usable fast charger is fast and unambiguous.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: When planning a 300‑mile highway trip, the route planner presents at least one compatible fast charger within each 150‑mile segment, including connector/compatibility info and estimated availability; in a usability test the median time to identify and confirm a suitable charger is ≤10 seconds (95% of trials).
assumptions: Navigation has access to up‑to‑date public charger metadata (connector type, network) and charger status APIs where available.
Trip planner can filter by vehicle compatibility and user preferences.
uncertainties: Third‑party charger data quality and availability varies by region; some regions may not meet the 150‑mile expectation.
Network availability may change in real time and require graceful fallbacks.

drafts.title: Offer at least one powertrain option that delivers ≥600 miles real‑world range per fill/charge
drafts.description: Customers who prioritize long range can choose a 5 Series configuration that delivers at least 600 miles of real‑world driving on a single tank or full charge so long trips need fewer fuel/charge stops.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: At least one production powertrain option achieves ≥600 miles on a single tank or full charge in an independent mixed-route real‑world validation (representative highway/city driving profile), verified on the same test procedure used for consumer-range claims.
assumptions: This target can be achieved with an internal‑combustion or hybrid powertrain variant rather than requiring a BEV with currently unavailable energy density.
Real‑world validation uses an agreed test protocol (mixed highway/city) comparable to current EPA or WLTP derived real‑world tests.
uncertainties: A BEV achieving 600+ miles may not be feasible within 3–5 years without major battery energy-density breakthroughs.
Customer expectations conflate 'one tank' (ICE) and 'one charge' (BEV); product communication must clarify which powertrain achieves the target.

drafts.scope_reason: Regulatory type approval / homologation request—out of scope for product-level customer outcome specification.
